text:
great video, I think about this a lot. In the future we will have RT/lumen/pathtracing to handle perfect lighting, Nanite to handle perfect objects and AI is coming in to help with animations and... better AI for NPCS. We are soon hitting 4k, 150fps with all the bells and whistles. No the 4090 can't do it yet, the 4090 is probably half the speed of the card we need to actually do it, but a 2x faster GPU is likely just the flagship of 2 or at most 3 generations down the line. the 6090 or 7090 will be that GPU, then beyond that do we actually need more GPU power? what is there to be gained?

We can only push things so far, scenes can get more and more elaborate and realistic looking, or impressive looking. Just keep adding detail to effects that don't need it. Make worlds ridiculously lush and full. Ok sure, so games get ridiculously dense but that is still not going to be enough to hold back gpu power for more than a couple generations beyond that. So a 8090 or 9090 and then what? Nvidia will try and push some BS feature that barely improves things and costs a ton of power and you don't need it. 8k resolution will get pushed, 360hz will get pushed, but it's all diminishing returns.

What will happen, I think, and we are already seeing it, is very CPU intensive games. Yes we make the worlds as beautiful as we can and hit a wall of diminishing returns around 2030, however games can have much much more going on. Big Vram, Big 3d V-cache, Big Ram, Fast Memory, Beefy CPU to simulate whole ecosystems, to simulate entire armies, to simulate entire cities, to simulate AI intellegence NPCs. That is the future beyond making games pretty, and that is the real limit to gaming for hopefully most of my life, making evermore complex things. Because we are absolutetly reaching the point of diminishing returns in visuals alone.

I think the good news is that in the next 8 years we will get to see some really nice growth visually and for PC hardware to get much better with 4k RT. The smart move to make is to understand where to draw the line on performance because hardware is getting super expensive on the GPU side and they will be pushing 8K which you don't need at all.

text:
We are indeed at the 90%+ mark in visual fidelity. But don't forget some critical factors.

1) The missing 10% can make a big difference in crossing the Uncanny Valley, especially in areas like human models in story-rich games with professional voice/mocap acting. Imagine a game where NPC is like the woman in the Unity "Enemies" demo.

2) Ray tracing is a big part of that missing 10%, and when done right (still needs a couple of GPU gens) it's a huge improvement in most other aspects of realism. Our brains are just too hardwired for the way light works in the real world, we unconsciously notice the smallest lies from rasterization tricks.

3) If we are at 90% in visuals, we're still barely breaking the 10% in physical realism. I want a game where my pants look wet and saggy after crossing a shallow river, without game designers having to specifically program that, just a natural consequence of proper simulation of how cloth works. I want a game where I'll break a chair and it splits down in pieces in a realistic way depending on the position and force of impact and the materials it is made off, and the fragments remain in the game instead of magically disappearing in seconds. Notice that there are game design challenges with this, e.g. you can trivialize or break platforming/traversal problems with weapons that can destroy almost every wall; but then games simply have to be better designed, at least ones that are not over-the-top power fantasies where you can have a shoulder-mounted nuke launcher.

Be careful: there is Samsung Mobile, Samsung Display, and Samsung Electronics.
Mobile is displays for phones/tablets
Display is for large-format displays (display walls and stadium displays)
Electronics is for consumer TVs, Fridge displays, etc.
So when "Samsung" is doing something you always need to figure out what division is doing it.
